result: DMD is an X-linked disease caused by dystrophin mutations that leads to progressive muscle deterioration, cardiac involvement, and arrhythmias, but the mechanisms underlying arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death are poorly understood.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 establish the clinical background of DMD through well-cited literature. These claims describe established knowledge about DMD pathophysiology, cardiac complications, and the knowledge gap regarding arrhythmia mechanisms. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior work.

result: The dystrophin-associated protein complex (DAPC) scaffolds ion channels including NaV1.5 and Kir2.1, and absence of dystrophin disrupts ion channel function in mdx mice, with NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 mutually modulating each other's surface expression.
evaluation: Claims C8-C15 summarize prior work establishing the role of DAPC in ion channel regulation. All claims are supported by citations to published literature. This provides the mechanistic foundation for the current study's hypothesis about channelosome dysfunction in DMD.

result: Three DMD patients (two hemizygous males and one heterozygous female) with different dystrophin mutations developed severe cardiomyopathy with ventricular arrhythmias; detailed clinical histories including ECG abnormalities, ventricular tachycardia, and heart failure are documented.
evaluation: Claims C31-C49 provide detailed clinical characterization of the three DMD patients from whom iPSC-CMs were derived. The clinical data including ECG findings (Figure 1), genetic mutations, and disease progression are well-documented. This establishes the clinical relevance of the model system.

result: iPSC-CMs from hemizygous DMD males lack full-length dystrophin protein (DP427), while heterozygous female iPSC-CMs show variable dystrophin expression, as confirmed by western blot and immunostaining.
evaluation: Claims C50-C58 are supported by western blot data (Figure 2a,b) and immunostaining (Figure 2e) showing absence of dystrophin in hemizygous males and variable expression in the heterozygous female. Statistical significance is reported (p=0.0001 for males, p=0.5864 for female vs control). The genetic mutations are characterized.

result: Micropatterning iPSC-CMs on Matrigel-coated PDMS produces cylindrical-shaped, binucleated cells with organized sarcomeres and mature electrophysiological properties (MDP -70 to -80 mV, APD 200-300 ms), facilitating patch-clamp experiments.
evaluation: Claims C59-C64 describe the micropatterning methodology and its effects on cell maturation. The approach is supported by citations (C59-C60) and experimental observations (Figure 2c,d). The electrophysiological parameters indicating maturation are documented in subsequent figures. This methodological advance is important for the study's experimental design.

result: DMD iPSC-CMs from all three patients showed abnormal action potential profiles with significantly reduced dV/dtmax compared to two control lines, while APD90 was unchanged; Male 2 showed reduced overshoot and amplitude, and the female showed depolarized MDP.
evaluation: Claims C67-C72 are supported by patch-clamp data in Figure 3 with statistical analysis. The reduction in dV/dtmax is significant across all DMD groups. The data show consistency between two control lines and differences among DMD patients, suggesting mutation-specific effects. Sample sizes are provided.

result: Conduction velocity was reduced by ~50% in hemizygous DMD iPSC-CM monolayers (27-29 cm/s vs 56 cm/s in control) and even more in heterozygous female monolayers (18 cm/s), with the female showing focal discharges and reentry; these changes occurred without alterations in connexin43 expression.
evaluation: Claims C73-C80 are supported by optical mapping data (Figure 4) and western blot for Cx43 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The CV measurements are quantified with error bars. The arrhythmia patterns in the female are documented with activation maps. The absence of Cx43 changes is important for mechanistic interpretation.

result: Peak INa density was significantly reduced in all DMD iPSC-CMs (hemizygous males: -14 to -15 pA/pF; heterozygous female: -11 pA/pF) compared to controls (-27 to -38 pA/pF), while biophysical properties and cell capacitance were unchanged.
evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by patch-clamp data (Figure 5a,b) with statistical comparisons across multiple groups. The reduction in INa is consistent across DMD patients. The preservation of biophysical properties and cell size (capacitance) indicates the defect is in channel density rather than gating or cell size.

result: ICa,L was unaltered in hemizygous and heterozygous DMD iPSC-CMs under the experimental conditions used.
evaluation: Claim C88 is supported by patch-clamp data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). This finding contrasts with some prior studies (C86-C87) but is clearly documented. The authors acknowledge the discrepancy and suggest methodological differences may explain it.

result: IK1 density at -120 mV was significantly reduced in hemizygous DMD iPSC-CMs (Male 1: -1.0 pA/pF; Male 2: -1.2 pA/pF) compared to controls (-3.2 and -2.6 pA/pF), while heterozygous female cells showed high variability without significant difference.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by patch-clamp data (Figure 5c,d). The reduction in IK1 is statistically significant in hemizygous males. The high variability in the heterozygous female is attributed to variable dystrophin expression (C93), which is a reasonable interpretation given the immunostaining data (C58).

result: SCN5A and KCNJ2 mRNA expression was upregulated in hemizygous DMD iPSC-CMs and in cardiac tissue from a Becker MD patient, suggesting a compensatory phenomenon, while CACNA1C was unchanged.
evaluation: Claims C95-C98 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3). The upregulation of SCN5A and KCNJ2 despite reduced current densities suggests post-transcriptional regulation. The consistency with Becker MD tissue strengthens the interpretation of a general compensatory mechanism.

result: Total NaV1.5 protein was reduced in DMD iPSC-CMs while total Kir2.1 was unchanged; biotinylation assays showed reduced membrane NaV1.5 (Male 2 only) and Kir2.1 (both males), indicating trafficking defects.
evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by western blot and biotinylation data (Figure 5—figure supplement 4). The differential effects on total vs membrane protein suggest trafficking defects. However, the biotinylation result for NaV1.5 is significant only in Male 2, which is somewhat inconsistent with the functional data showing reduced INa in both males.

result: In heterozygous female iPSC-CMs, NaV1.5 total and membrane protein levels were not different from control despite dramatically reduced INa density, attributed to large variability in dystrophin expression.
evaluation: Claims C104-C105 present a puzzling finding: normal NaV1.5 protein levels but reduced INa. The explanation of variability in dystrophin expression is plausible given the immunostaining data, but the biochemical assays may not capture cell-to-cell heterogeneity that patch-clamp does. Additional single-cell protein analysis would strengthen this interpretation.

result: Transfection of SNTA1 (α1-syntrophin) in Male 1 DMD iPSC-CMs increased membrane NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 (by WGA colocalization), restored INa and IK1 densities, and normalized action potential parameters (hyperpolarized MDP, increased dV/dtmax and amplitude, abbreviated APD90).
evaluation: Claims C109-C114 are supported by immunostaining (Figure 6c,d) and patch-clamp data (Figure 7). The rescue of both protein localization and functional parameters by a single DAPC component is a key finding. Statistical significance is shown. However, the rescue was tested in only one patient line (Male 1), limiting generalizability.

result: SNTA1 expression in Male 1 iPSC-CM monolayers showed a tendency to increase conduction velocity toward control, significantly shortened APD, and eliminated arrhythmia inducibility in 9/10 monolayers.
evaluation: Claims C115-C119 are supported by optical mapping data (Figure 8). The CV rescue showed variability but a clear trend. The APD shortening was statistically significant. The dramatic reduction in arrhythmia inducibility (9/10 vs 1/10 in control) is a strong functional outcome. The authors appropriately note the variability in CV rescue.

result: Male 1 DMD iPSC-CMs showed defective contractility (prolonged shortening/relaxation, reduced slope and amplitude), which was rescued by SNTA1 expression, highlighting the importance of the NaV1.5-Kir2.1 channelosome for excitation-contraction coupling.
evaluation: Claims C120-C122 are supported by contractility assay data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The rescue of contractility by SNTA1 links electrical and mechanical function. This extends the findings beyond electrophysiology to show functional consequences for cardiac contraction.

result: iPSC-CMs from DMD patients recapitulate key electrophysiological features including reduced INa and IK1, abnormal action potentials, slowed conduction, and arrhythmias; membrane NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 were reduced in hemizygous but not heterozygous cells; SNTA1 transfection rescued these defects, suggesting reduced excitability underlies arrhythmogenesis in DMD.
evaluation: Claims C16-C30 summarize the main findings from the abstract. These are supported by the detailed experimental data in Figures 3-8. The conclusion that reduced excitability underlies arrhythmogenesis (C30) is well-supported by the convergent evidence from action potentials, ion currents, conduction velocity, and arrhythmia inducibility. The rescue by SNTA1 provides strong mechanistic support.

result: Patient-specific iPSC-CMs recapitulate DMD cardiomyopathy features; the defects result from NaV1.5-α1-syntrophin-Kir2.1 channelosome dysfunction due to DAPC disruption; SNTA1 transfection restores function and prevents arrhythmias; this is the first comprehensive mechanistic demonstration of arrhythmogenesis in human DMD.
evaluation: Claims C123-C130 present the main conclusions of the Discussion. These are well-supported by the experimental data. The claim of being 'first' (C130) is reasonable given the comprehensive nature of the study combining patient-specific iPSCs, detailed electrophysiology, and rescue experiments. The mechanistic link between DAPC disruption and channelosome dysfunction is strongly supported.

result: INa density in heterozygous female iPSC-CMs was even more reduced than in hemizygous males, correlating with prolonged QRS on ECG; this is attributed to heterogeneity from random X-inactivation creating a mosaic of cells with variable dystrophin expression, predisposing to arrhythmias.
evaluation: Claims C170-C174 present an important finding about heterozygous females. The reduced INa (C170) is supported by patch-clamp data (Figure 5). The correlation with clinical ECG (C171) is documented (Figure 1c). The X-inactivation explanation (C172-C173) is supported by immunostaining showing variable dystrophin (C58) and cited literature. The inference about arrhythmia susceptibility (C174) is logical given the electrical heterogeneity.

result: The study has limitations: iPSC-CMs differ from adult cardiomyocytes; results may not generalize to other dystrophin mutations like Becker MD; rescue experiments were limited to Male 1; however, the channelosome defects were similar across all three DMD patients.
evaluation: Claims C186-C189 acknowledge important limitations. These are appropriate and honest assessments. The limitation that rescue was tested in only one patient (C188) is significant but mitigated by the similarity of defects across patients (C189). The inability to generalize to Becker MD (C187) is a reasonable caveat.
